titles: How a Two-Person Coffee Roastery Got 4,000 Subscribers With No Ads
212 Emails on a Clipboard: How Kettle Lane Coffee Survived 2020
He Spent $1,800 on Instagram Ads and Got 11 Customers
The Skip-a-Month Button That Cut Subscription Churn From 9% to 4%
One Plain-Text Email Every Sunday Built a $32/Month Subscription
description:
Daniel Reyes runs Kettle Lane Coffee, a coffee subscription with 4,000 subscribers and no advertising. In this episode of Small Batch he explains how a clipboard of 212 email addresses and one plain-text email every Sunday became a $32-a-month subscription business, why three months of Instagram ads failed, and how a skip-a-month button took churn from 9% to 4%.

Chapters
00:00 A roastery with 4,000 subscribers and no ads
01:45 Selling 60 bags a week from a garage
05:10 The farmers market closes, and the clipboard list
08:30 The first Sunday email: 38 orders
12:20 $1,800 on Instagram ads for 11 customers
15:05 First dibs instead of discounts
18:40 Taking churn from 9% to 4% with a skip button
21:15 The $40,000 roaster mistake
24:30 What to do on Monday if you have no audience

Key points
- A list of 212 email addresses was enough to start. The first plain-text email brought in 38 orders.
- Three months of Instagram ads cost $1,800 and produced 11 customers, most of whom cancelled within two months.
- Kettle Lane does not discount. Subscribers get every new roast 48 hours before anyone else.
- Most cancellations came from people who still had coffee left. A one-click skip button took monthly churn from 9% to 4%.
- Daniel's advice: pick one channel and be boring about it for a year, and answer customer emails yourself.

Guest: Daniel Reyes, co-founder of Kettle Lane Coffee
Host: Maya Ortiz

shorts.title: $1,800 in ads, 11 customers
shorts.hook: This coffee roaster spent eighteen hundred dollars on Instagram ads and got eleven customers.
shorts.script: This coffee roaster spent eighteen hundred dollars on Instagram ads and got eleven customers. His name is Daniel Reyes and he runs Kettle Lane Coffee. In 2021 everyone told him he had to be on Instagram, so he ran ads for three months. Eleven people signed up, and most of them cancelled within two months. They had come for a discount and didn't know the company. In those same months his plain Sunday email was adding forty to fifty people a week, because customers kept forwarding it to friends. He stopped the ads and never went back. Kettle Lane now has four thousand subscribers.
shorts.caption: Three months of ads brought 11 customers. A plain weekly email was bringing 40 to 50 a week. Full conversation with Daniel Reyes on the channel.

shorts.title: The skip-a-month button
shorts.hook: Kettle Lane Coffee was losing nine percent of its subscribers every single month.
shorts.script: Kettle Lane Coffee was losing nine percent of its subscribers every single month. So the founders asked people why they were cancelling. The most common answer had nothing to do with the coffee. It was: I still have some left from last time. Customers weren't unhappy. They were full. So Daniel Reyes added one button to the account page: skip a month. One click, no questions, no are-you-sure page. Monthly churn went from nine percent to four. If people are leaving your subscription, ask them why before you offer a discount. The fix might be a button.
shorts.caption: Their subscribers were not unhappy, they just had coffee left. One button took churn from 9% to 4%.

shorts.title: 212 emails on a clipboard
shorts.hook: In March 2020 the farmers market where Daniel Reyes sold his coffee closed with a week's notice.
shorts.script: In March 2020 the farmers market where Daniel Reyes sold his coffee closed with a week's notice. That stall was his whole business. What he had left was a clipboard. For a year his wife Ana had asked customers to write down their email address. There were two hundred and twelve on it. He sent them a plain email: here's what we roasted this week, reply if you want a bag. Thirty-eight people ordered. He sent another the next Sunday, and one every Sunday since. That list is now four thousand subscribers paying thirty-two dollars a month.
shorts.caption: A clipboard at a market stall turned into 4,000 subscribers. Daniel Reyes of Kettle Lane Coffee on Small Batch.

linkedin_post:
I interviewed Daniel Reyes of Kettle Lane Coffee this week. He and his wife Ana have 4,000 coffee subscribers and have not run an ad since 2021.

Their business had to start over in March 2020, when the farmers market they sold at closed with a week's notice. What they had was a clipboard with 212 email addresses on it. Daniel sent a plain-text email: here is this week's coffee, reply if you want a bag. 38 people ordered. He has sent one every Sunday since.

Three things I wrote down:

1. They ran Instagram ads for three months. $1,800 bought 11 customers, and most cancelled within two months.

2. They never discount. Subscribers get each new roast 48 hours early instead.

3. Churn was 9% a month until they asked people why they were leaving. The answer was "I still have coffee left." A skip-a-month button took it to 4%.

His advice for anyone starting without an audience: pick one channel and be boring about it for a year.

The full episode of Small Batch is on the channel.
